title: Algorithms are recipes for thinking
description: An algorithm is just a set of steps guaranteed to finish a job — you use them when you sort laundry, follow a recipe or find a name in a list.

body.heading: A word with a person's name inside
paragraphs: The word algorithm comes from the Latinised name of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a scholar in 9th-century Baghdad whose books on calculation taught Europe the Hindu-Arabic numerals we still use. His name became the word for any step-by-step method of solving a problem.

An algorithm must be precise enough that no judgement is needed mid-step, and it must finish. A cake recipe is nearly an algorithm — 'bake until golden' leaves a little judgement in, which is why recipes still sometimes fail us.

body.heading: Algorithms you already know
paragraphs: Searching a printed phone book teaches the most elegant trick in computing. Open it in the middle: if your name comes later, throw away the entire first half. Repeat. Each step halves the search, so a million entries fall in about twenty steps. That is binary search, and computers use it constantly.

Sorting works the same way. Dealing cards into order one at a time, or splitting a pile into smaller piles and merging them sorted — these are real sorting algorithms, differing only in how much work they make you do.

body.heading: Why steps matter
paragraphs: The study of algorithms is mostly the study of effort: how does the work grow as the problem grows? A method fine for ten names may be hopeless for ten billion. Choosing the right steps is the quiet heart of computer science.

When people argue about 'the algorithm' in daily life, they usually mean a company's recipe for ranking posts or videos. Remember the humble original: a recipe for thinking, written so carefully that even a machine — or a tired human — can follow it to the end.

takeaway: Algorithms are finishable recipes for problems, named after a Baghdad scholar, and the cleverest ones win by throwing away half the work at every step.
